Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-12
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Morgan Lee (Redwood AE), Alex Chen (Redwood SE), Sanjay Patel (Redwood Product), Jane Ortega (EdgeScale Infra Lead), Ravi Kumar (EdgeScale ML), Liam O'Neil (EdgeScale SRE), Mei Tan (EdgeScale Security)

Transcript:
[00:00] Morgan (AE): hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. we wanted to focus today's deep dive on the scheduler behavior at the edge—especially eviction and batching tradeoffs. alex will lead, i'm just uh here to coordinate.
[00:18] Jane (EdgeScale): thanks Morgan. our main pain is that our edge racks have smaller GPUs and when traffic spikes, latency tails blow up. we suspect kv cache churn and some aggressive seq packing is causing GPU memory thrash.
[00:33] Alex (SE): yeah that's exactly what we've seen in similar setups. quick clarifier: are you running Redwood Private on-prem with the VPC overlay? or is this a more air-gapped image?
[00:42] Jane: it's VPC-connected but bandwidth between racks is limited, and we do a customer-managed private control plane. so, we need configs that don't assume high cross-node IO.
[00:52] Sanjay (Product): also to flag, do you currently pin model versions or do you let the scheduler fallback to a quantized variant?
[00:58] Ravi (ML): right now we pin to the base float16 model for quality. we tried the int8 quantized variant but saw weird hallucination regressions on some prompts.
[01:10] Alex: got it. so we should avoid automatic fallback to lower-precision unless you want that. our focus will be scheduler knobs: continuous-batching window sizes, max_num_seqs, token caps, and eviction thresholds for the KV cache.
[01:22] Liam (SRE): one quick thing — the incidents happen when we see 3x baseline RPS sustained for ~120s, then a handful of long sequences show up and things degrade. the scheduler starts packing aggressively to keep throughput up and then memory spikes.
[01:38] Alex: classic. there are a couple of levers. high-level: (1) reduce max_num_seqs to reserve headroom for long sequences, (2) throttle aggressive continuous-batching window expansion during bursts, (3) tune kv cache eviction to favor long-lived prefixes, (4) token_limit guards per-tenant.
[01:54] Jane: can you unpack the max_num_seqs tradeoff? we've seen docs say higher max_num_seqs -> better throughput but also tail latency risk.
[02:03] Alex: totally. think of max_num_seqs as the scheduler's packing capacity. larger values let the GPU run with more in-flight sequences which boosts throughput up to GPU saturation. but with small-GPU memory, each additional sequence increases KV cache pressure. When memory crosses eviction thresholds, you get more cache misses and cold KV insert churn which spikes latency.
[02:24] Ravi: so what's your recommended starting point for our node size? we have A10-equivalent with 20GB usable.
[02:30] Alex: for 20GB I'd recommend starting at max_num_seqs = 32 to 48, not the default 96 we use in big-hosted clusters. also set per-request token_limits to 512 by default and use a soft token-ceiling for unexpected long requests.
[02:46] Morgan: note — we can put a guardrail so requests > 512 tokens are routed to a special pool with more reserved memory or rate-limited.
[02:54] Jane: ok that helps. what about continuous-batching window? we've observed the scheduler widens the window aggressively during light load which sometimes causes odd batching behavior when burst occurs.
[03:06] Alex: the continuous-batching window has two knobs: base_window_ms and max_expand_ms. base_window sets the normal batching latency target; max_expand controls how much the window can grow to optimize throughput. on small nodes, you want a smaller base_window_ms (e.g., 6-10ms) and conservative max_expand (maybe 30-50ms) so it doesn't absorb too many long sequences during spikes.
[03:26] Liam: those numbers seem tight; will that kill throughput too much?
[03:30] Alex: there is a throughput reduction but it's more predictable. the key is to combine smaller windows with a dynamic backpressure policy: if GPU mem crossing 80% then reduce window to base immediately and start preferring small batches.
[03:43] Jane: how do we detect the GPU mem crossing? we don't want to rely solely on infra metrics that may lag.
[03:49] Alex: Redwood's runtime exposes instantaneous mem signals from the allocator; the scheduler can subscribe and apply backpressure in <200ms. in your on-prem image we can enable the telemetry hook that emits mem headroom.
[03:59] Ravi: can we see example thresholds? like mem>80% do X, mem>90% do Y.
[04:04] Alex: yes. recommended: mem>80% -> reduce max_num_seqs by 25% and set window to base; mem>90% -> stop expansion, enable conservative packing (max_num_seqs=16) and reject large token requests to protected pool. also trigger KV cache aggressive pruning for low-hit prefixes.
[04:22] Mei (Security): quick interjection: any change to request routing or rejecting large requests will be logged? we need audit trail for tokens dropped and rerouted for compliance.
[04:30] Alex: yes audit logs are emitted; we can add a flag to log token-level decisions and reason codes (eg: REJECT_TOKEN_LIMIT, ROUTE_TO_RESERVED_POOL).
[04:38] Morgan: and that ties into the next steps—Morgan to share the security brief and logging excerpt.
[04:43] Jane: good. shifting to KV cache — how do we reduce churn? our pattern is many short queries, then a few long multi-turns. KV thrashing seems huge.
[04:54] Alex: two strategies: a) favor LRU with priority pins for prefixes that cross a longevity threshold (e.g., if a prefix seen >10 times in last 10 minutes, pin weight++), b) use proactive prewarm for predicted hot prefixes during deployments or expected spikes. prewarm is cheaper than repopulation.
[05:11] Ravi: for prewarm, how do we predict prefixes without leaking PII or customer data across tenants?
[05:18] Alex: keep predictions on-device; you can feed anonymized prefix hashes from your traffic replay. Redwood's warmup tool accepts hashed keys and warms only matching kernel structures without storing raw text. we also offer a TTL-based pin if you can't precompute.
[05:30] Jane: ok that fits our privacy needs. about eviction thresholds, is there a risk of the scheduler evicting prefixes needed for long-running sessions?
[05:39] Alex: yes that's the tradeoff. we propose a two-tier eviction policy: short-lived prefixes evicted aggressively under pressure, long-lived prefixes flagged as protected for X minutes after last use. that protects multi-turn sessions.
[05:53] Liam: what's the ops cost? does that increase RAM meta-info?
[05:56] Alex: negligible; it's mostly a small metadata bit per prefix. we measured <2% additional memory on a 20GB node.
[06:03] Jane: great. could you walk us through a failure scenario and the sequence of scheduler reactions? maybe show timelines?
[06:09] Alex: sure — i shared a quick timeline slide (note: slide deck link in chat). but verbally: baseline load at 200 RPS, small batches, KV hitrate ~85%. a 3x sustained surge hits, long sequences arrive, mem climbs to 82% -> scheduler reduces window and lowers max_num_seqs; but if long sequences continue, mem hits 90% -> scheduler triggers conservative-mode: reserve a small protected pool, enable token re-routing, start aggressive eviction for short prefixes. if that still fails we fallback to a compat model variant on a less busy node (if available).
[06:41] Ravi: you mentioned compat variant fallback — we don't want quality regressions. can we instead route long requests to a prewarmed node only?
[06:49] Alex: yes, that's the recommended pattern for on-prem: maintain a tiny reserved pool (1-2 GPUs) pinned with prewarmed KV cache for long seqs. it costs a little but avoids spilling quality.
[06:58] Jane: what's the best way to size that reserved pool?
[07:02] Alex: size it by anticipated concurrent long seqs. e.g., if you expect 5 concurrent long seqs, reserve capacity equal to 2-3 sequences per GPU depending on model. our bench can help estimate.
[07:12] Morgan: alex, can you talk about quantization effects? they had hallucination before. any perf/quality tradeoffs we should note?
[07:17] Alex: absolutely. quantization (int8) reduces memory footprint and speeds inference, which improves throughput and reduces mem pressure. however, some prompt-sensitive workloads show small quality deltas — often fixable with calibration or selective quantization of specific layers. we advise a two-stage approach: run an int8 bench on a subset of openset prompts; if delta < tolerance, enable; otherwise use mixed-precision: quantize only feed-forward layers and keep attention in fp16.
[07:43] Ravi: can Redwood provide tools for automatic calibration?
[07:47] Alex: yes we have an offline calibration harness that uses a small labeled prompt set to derive per-layer scales. we'll share the harness and a recommended 1000-prompt calibration suite.
[07:55] Jane: this is helpful. what about token limits enforcement — can we set soft vs hard limits? we don't want to abruptly terminate an in-progress conversation.
[08:03] Alex: there are three modes: hard_reject (500-token hard cut), soft_route (route to reserved pool and log), and graceful_trim (notify client and truncate oldest tokens then continue). recommended: soft_route as default, with grace for critical sessions to graceful_trim.
[08:18] Liam: from SRE lens we want deterministic behavior for SLAs — soft_route is good because it keeps latency bounded and allows logging for SLA ops.
[08:26] Mei: make sure logs show reason codes and we have RBAC access to those logs — security requirement.
[08:31] Morgan: we'll include logging and RBAC notes in the security brief.
[08:36] Alex: one more operational note: for on-prem we recommend enabling local prefetched KV snapshot during nightly low-load windows to keep hotspot prefixes warm; this reduces cold-start misses during morning spikes.
[08:48] Ravi: is that snapshot small? we don't want large storage cost.
[08:51] Alex: it's incremental; only hot prefixes. typical snapshots we saw were <200MB for a 20GB node.
[08:57] Jane: ok good. switching to benchmarks — can you propose a minimal bench plan to reproduce our incidents?
[09:03] Alex: yes: 1) replay test with 5k traces (we'll use your replay), 2) synthetic surge test: baseline 200 RPS ramp to 600 RPS sustained 120s with 10% long seqs, 3) cold vs warm KV tests with prewarm vs no prewarm, 4) quantized vs fp16 A/B. we'll run these with max_num_seqs=[32,48,64] and continuous window sets [8/40ms, 10/30ms, 6/50ms].
[09:31] Morgan: we'll log everything and provide the full results sheet. alex, can you run the first sweep on our lab cluster and then on customer hardware with their replay?
[09:39] Alex: yes — i can start on our lab cluster (p4d equiv) and then coordinate a remote bench on their image. need the replay and a small container image.
[09:47] Jane: we'll upload traces and grant access to a snapshot.
[09:50] Ravi: one more nuance — when you run with smaller max_num_seqs, do you expect CPU overhead to increase due to more scheduling churn?
[09:57] Alex: modestly. smaller batches increase per-request overhead on the scheduler thread, but it's usually <5% CPU delta. main cost is throughput drop, not CPU. we can offset with a slightly higher worker count.
[10:08] Liam: about node-to-node fallback — since your VPC bandwidth is limited, is remote fallback realistic?
[10:13] Alex: remote fallback is only recommended for low-latency links; for your topology we recommended local reserved pool instead of cross-rack fallback. remote fallback still works as an emergency but expect added latency.
[10:22] Jane: okay. any other production knobs we should consider?
[10:26] Alex: yes: token_bucket shaping to smooth burst arrivals at the front door, request prioritization windows for critical tenants, and an adaptive eviction policy that escalates from LRU to frequency-based under pressure.
[10:38] Ravi: token_bucket shaping is at the edge gateway layer — we can implement that. how do we set the bucket size?
[10:44] Alex: set burst_size to 2x baseline RPS and refill to baseline per second; monitor for 7 days and adjust.
[10:52] Morgan: ok wrapping up — recap and action items.
[10:55] Jane: quick question before we wrap: about prewarming hashed prefixes — will that affect our PII policies? we want the warmup process to avoid storing raw prefixes in Redwood logs.
[11:05] Alex: yes we will accept hashed indices and the warmup tool will not log raw text; logs only show prefix hashes and warmup success/failure. we'll include that in the security brief.
[11:13] Jane: perfect.
[11:15] Morgan: cool, thanks all. next steps: Alex to run initial lab benches and send config proposal; Morgan to send security brief and pricing sketch for reserved pool; EdgeScale to upload traces and telemetry.
[11:28] Jane: thanks everyone, looking forward to the bench results.
[11:32] (meeting ends)
